comments.author: @World-Discoveries26
comments.text: New Zealand’s isolation is incredible, but what fascinated me more was how people have built a comfortable, modern life surrounded by such powerful nature. The balance between the two feels very unique.

replies.author: @BestTravel2
replies.text: I’m so glad that balance stood out to you, it really is a defining feature of the modern Kiwi lifestyle!

comments.author: @ExploreTravelDocs
comments.text: I’ve always dreamed of visiting New Zealand, but videos like this make me wonder—is living there actually as peaceful and idyllic as it looks, or does the remote location get tough after a while? Would love to hear from locals or expats! 🏔👀

replies.author: @JuanitaRichards-c4t
replies.text: Its a great place to live..I've traveled and lived in a third world country, but I'd rather live here than anywhere else.

replies.author: @ExploreTravelDocs
replies.text: @GoodGeekery 😂 “Master the art of dodging tourists” made me laugh! But I totally get what you mean—the space and solitude sound like part of the appeal, especially on the South Island. Is there a quieter part of the South Island you’d personally recommend where you can still get that real sense of New Zealand without the crowds? 🇳🇿

replies.author: @GoodGeekery
replies.text: I vey much value the solitude the isolation can provide. Places like Auckland are little different to other large cities. Still, it's spread out with a better sense of space compared to the density of living conditions elsewhere though. The plus is that it doesn't take much to get away from that. South Island suits my way of being. Just develop the knack of dodging the tourists.

replies.author: @ExploreTravelDocs
replies.text: @BestTravel2 That’s exactly the side of New Zealand I was curious about. The scenery is what draws people in, but housing, groceries, and that sense of isolation are the things you only really understand once everyday life begins. 🇳🇿

replies.author: @BestTravel2
replies.text: Living in New Zealand involves real-world challenges like high costs for housing and groceries, along with the isolation of being at the edge of the world, which balances out the beautiful scenery.

comments.author: @LifewaysTravel
comments.text: New Zealand looks incredible, but I think people romanticize life there a little too much. Anyone disagree?

replies.author: @JuanitaRichards-c4t
replies.text: I wouldn't say romanticize...we just love our little corner of the world.  I've traveled and lived in a third world country but there is nowhere like NZ.  Many Americans have moved here and they love it.  Some have Youtube channels and they give an honest appraisal of our little country.

replies.author: @johnjamesmoses
replies.text: As a 76 year old New Zealander I thought the commentary was good. He mentioned both the upside and downside for people living here Housing in the cities is expensive, food can be too. Young people and families head to Australia for greater career prospects. On the upside we live in a beautiful country. If one enjoys the outdoors, hiking, the beach, boating, fishing, or whatever it is never far away and free to enjoy. Like Australia and Canada as former colonies of Britain we share the Westminster form of Government which serves us well.  I love New Zealand and often think how fortunate I am to have been born here

replies.author: @NicolaStainlay
replies.text: No, I thought the doco was pretty accurate, if not a touch gloomy compared with the idyllic childhood I had in the 1950s. We moved to Australia in the early 60s for better opportunities, in the same way New Zealanders are still doing, but my parents moved back in the late 80s, again just as so many are doing now. Our countries of our birth have a very strong pull.

comments.text: Just finished preparing a traditional Māori Hāngī feast with the family near Queenstown! Living down here means putting on extra thermals for sudden southern winds and driving miles between small towns. Could you handle living in a country where sheep outnumber humans and isolation is a way of life? 🇳🇿

replies.author: @JuanitaRichards-c4t
replies.text: My parents owned the Lake Hayes motels back in the 1980s....I lived in Dunedin and used to visit them to help out, another sister used to visit from Invercargill and 2 others sisters from Christchurch.  Eventually my parents moved to Amberley and the motels were sold and eventually knocked down.  I love hangi.....it's very hard to get these days unless you know someone who does them.

comments.author: @NicolaStainlay
comments.text: As an expat, to Australia Kiwi, this is quite an accurate picture of current life in New Zealand except for the pronunciation of two commonly-used terms. The Māori word for family groups ‘whanau’ is said ‘fanau’ and the weekender ‘bach’ is said ‘batch’.
